en.title: Ten Days, No Visa: What China's Transit-Free Opening to Vietnam Really Signals
en.subtitle: From 55 to 57 countries: how a technical visa adjustment became a soft footnote in China's peripheral diplomacy
en.summary: From 20 August 2026, Vietnamese and Kyrgyz citizens may use China's 240-hour transit visa-free policy and Hainan's 30-day entry waiver, lifting participant counts to 57 and 61. A modest tweak on paper, it is a soft instrument of Beijing's peripheral diplomacy — signalling goodwill through people's movement rather than ships, above all toward a rivalry-bound Vietnam. en.title: When Qixi Goes Overseas: How a Diaspora Holds Its Festival Between Romance and Tradition
en.subtitle: From hotpot in Buenos Aires to the “Seventh Maiden” rites in Malacca, Qixi now carries both romance and tradition in overseas Chinese communities — an anchor of identity and a quiet act of soft power.
en.summary: China News Service's August 19 phone interviews with four diaspora figures record how they marked Qixi: hotpot in Buenos Aires' Chinatown and a new generation's identity, the pipa piece "Butterfly Lovers" before Turin's Royal Palace, the Hokkien community in Malacca calling Qixi "Qijie Dan / Qiniangma Sheng" and performing child-protection rites for children under 16, and a Chinese-heritage teacher in the US folding the festival into cross-cultural classes. Once overseas, Qixi holds commercial romance alongside older rites of qiqiao and child protection — the diaspora may be preserving the "thicker" version the homeland has thinned.

en.title: "A Reliable Partner in Southeast Asia": Min Aung Hlaing's Sixth Moscow Trip and Myanmar's Geopolitical Escape Hatch
en.subtitle: On August 18, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing told Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin that "Myanmar is a reliable partner for Russia in Southeast Asia." Behind the diplomatic phrasing lies how an internationally isolated junta has used Moscow to pry open its own diplomatic space.
en.summary: On August 18, Myanmar's Senior General Min Aung Hlaing made his sixth trip to Moscow — and first as civilian president — telling Putin that Myanmar is Russia's reliable partner in Southeast Asia. A five-year military pact, small nuclear plants and arms sales sketch a partnership under sanctions; an isolated junta uses Moscow for weapons and diplomatic cover while turning its predicament into bargaining chips. en.title: Semiconductors Lift Two Nations Into the "Upper-Middle-Income" Club — and the Harder Climb Ahead
en.subtitle: In the World Bank's July classification, Vietnam and the Philippines crossed the US$4,636 per-capita GNI threshold for the first time, riding a wave of semiconductor and electronics exports. The real test, analysts say, is escaping the middle-income trap that has ensnared their neighbours.
en.summary: In the World Bank's July classification, Vietnam and the Philippines crossed the US$4,636 per-capita GNI threshold for the first time, buoyed by semiconductor and electronics exports. But Nikkei Asia warns that reaching high income requires shedding reliance on cheap labour and moving up the value chain. Thailand and Indonesia have fallen into the middle-income trap, while Malaysia leveraged semiconductors to recover. Vietnam and the Philippines have cleared the first threshold; whether they can upgrade assembly into creation is the real race.
en.imageAlt: Workers in blue uniforms at an assembly line in a large factory, symbolising manufacturing upgrade

en.title: When a Wartime Chinese Restaurant Took the Spotlight: Diaspora, Soft Power, and the Politics of "Just Eat Well"
en.subtitle: Wen Muye's film grossed 900 million yuan in six days; Shen Teng's Northeastern cook sails to a war-torn Middle East to run a Chinese kitchen and feed orphaned children. Its real prototype: Shenzhen merchants who opened the "China Dragon" restaurant in Iraq in 2003. Why does a film about an overseas Chinese eatery unsettle our settled image of the diaspora?
en.summary: Welcome to Dragon Restaurant earned 900 million yuan in six days, staging its story in a Chinese restaurant amid a Middle Eastern war, where a cook uses hot meals to shelter war orphans. Its prototype is Liu Lei and Shuai Xuejun, Shenzhen merchants who ran the "China Dragon" eatery in Iraq in 2003. The piece argues that Chinese food went global long beyond Southeast Asia, and the film pivots the overseas-Chinese narrative from "roots" and "survival" toward the world's conflict zones — asserting a soft power of "harmony as the highest good" while warning against flattening the diaspora into a footnote of soft power.
en.imageAlt: A chef in a white uniform cooking at the stove, echoing the 'overseas Chinese restaurant' as a diaspora symbol

en.title: From a Fleeing Child to a Homecoming Soldier: A Malaysian Returned Chinese and the Century-Long Echo of a Diasporic China
en.subtitle: The memoir of 90-year-old Xiao Siming — who fled Japanese atrocities in Nanyang, sailed home in 1949, and enlisted in 1953 — is more than a family story. It is a window into how Southeast Asia's Chinese communities have always negotiated belonging between two shores.
en.summary: Xiao Siming, a 90-year-old returned overseas Chinese from Malaysia, fled Japanese atrocities in Nanyang as a child, sailed home in 1949, and enlisted in 1953, serving eleven years around Shanghai. His personal arc rhymes with the devotion of the Nanyang Mechanics and Tan Kah Kee's fundraising, yet his family now numbers over two hundred in Malaysia — 'roots in China' coexisting with a local kin network, the real condition of Southeast Asian Chinese today. Memory is both a human channel and a risk of being flattened into a brief for extraterritorial loyalty.
en.imageAlt: A narrow Penang street hung with red Chinese lanterns, echoing the everyday life of the Nanyang overseas Chinese

en.title: Declared as “Agricultural Waste”
en.subtitle: Nine Malaysian firms under investigation in Pontian — a cross-border culvert opened by one line on a customs form, and arbitrage beneath a special economic zone
en.summary: Construction waste believed to originate in Singapore has been illegally dumped in kampungs across Pontian, Johor, for two years, with nine Malaysian companies under investigation; the material entered via the Second Link declared as “agricultural waste.” A RM100,000 (roughly US$24,000) fine ceiling against two years of hauling revenue shows deterrence functioning as a fee rather than a constraint. en.subtitle: Shantou University launches its fifth country oral-history project, recording twenty prominent Teochew leaders in Singapore
en.summary: Shantou University's Institute of Area Studies and Overseas Chinese has launched its fifth country oral-history project in Singapore, conducting in-depth interviews with twenty prominent Teochew leaders on their migration, entrepreneurship and local contribution. The team also visited landmarks such as Chui Huay Lim Club, Thung Wai Hospital and the Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan, linking fieldwork to diaspora reality. en.title: Two Hours a Day: How a Philippine Classroom Timetable Became a Security File
en.subtitle: The Philippine defense secretary, citing an American think-tank report, has filed Chinese-language teacher training under national security. A dispute about Mandarin lessons is reopening a question the Philippines sealed fifty years ago.
en.summary: On 29 July 2026, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., citing a US think-tank SeaLight report, branded Jinan University's teacher training for Philippine Chinese schools as 'huge evidence' of schools being misused, prompting the cancellation of a three-week August fieldwork.
